references.text: Isaiah prophesies that the Messiah is anointed to proclaim good news to the poor – the same theme Jesus addresses in his beatitude of the poor.
Matthew's parallel beatitude: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.' This is the closest parallel to Luke 6:20 in the Sermon on the Mount.
Jesus answers John's disciples that the poor have the gospel preached to them – a sign that God's kingdom has come, confirming the promise in Luke 6:20.
Jesus reads from Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth and declares that he is anointed to preach the gospel to the poor, which forms the background for the beatitude in 6:20.
Jesus tells John's disciples that the poor have the good news preached to them – the fulfillment of the promise toward which the beatitude points.
James writes that God has chosen those who are poor in the world's eyes to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him – parallel to the promise in Luke 6:20.
The psalm describes the righteous king who will judge the poor with justice and save the needy – a messianic foreshadowing of God's kingdom care for the poor.
God dwells with the one who is crushed and lowly in spirit, to give life to the humble – this underscores God's closeness to the poor and humble, as Luke 6:20 promises them the kingdom of God.
The Lord looks on the one who is afflicted and downcast in spirit – an Old Testament background for why the poor and humble hold a special place with God.
Jesus says to the church in Smyrna: 'I know your affliction and your poverty – yet you are rich.' This reflects the paradox in Luke 6:20 that the poor possess the kingdom of God.
